turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
What I bring is about eighteen years of keeping infrastructure running, and a strong dislike of hearing it called "free." Anyone who says open infrastructure is "cost-free" is either naïve or disingenuous. It erases the people who keep the machines running, answer the questions and manage the services. So the first honest answer to "who pays?" is that somebody always does. Usually it's staff nobody sees.

Second, I have to own a mistake. In POSI we said you can't sell data, so earn your revenue from services. Looking back, that was naive. It asks you to find services valuable enough that people will pay for them, but not so valuable that they're essential to the scholarly record. That's close to impossible. I keep asking whether we need diamond open access infrastructure instead: endowments, pooled contingency funds, proper public support.

Third, there's a new cost. Badly behaved scrapers, a lot of them vibe-coded, are hammering open APIs. Open providers pay for that in bandwidth and staff time, and the people generating the load mostly don't know they're doing it.

For the summit, I'd hold one line firmly. Whatever payment scheme comes out of this, it mustn't close off the data, because open data is what gives a community the option to walk away. I don't have a settled view on licensing content to model builders.

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
Geoff's right that somebody always pays. At the Press we've tried to make that visible. Direct to Open works as a collective subsidy: libraries that would have bought our monographs anyway fund them instead, and once enough commit, that year's list goes open. We published the numbers. We also have an open knowledge endowment, seeded by Arcadia, so I'd second Geoff's point about endowments. They're what let us take risks on diamond OA.

On who gets paid, I'd bring in authors. In 2024 we surveyed about 6,000 of our book authors. They aren't anti-AI. But only 3% supported completely unregulated training use. They want consent, attribution and compensation. Attribution isn't vanity in scholarship. It's how we know whose judgment underwrites a claim.

For the summit I'd take three things. Default to opt-in licensing, with short deals renegotiated every couple of years. Favor retrieval over pre-training, because retrieval keeps provenance intact. And don't assume "open for reading" means "open for training." One of our authors said open access "should not mean Open to Theft." Open access policy without funding for nonprofits drove consolidation. I don't want AI deals repeating that, with only the biggest publishers at the table and smaller presses left behind. Geoff, I agree metadata should stay open. Content is a separate question.

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
I should say first that I haven't worked on scholarly infrastructure. Geoff and Amy know that ground far better than I do. What I can speak to is the other side of the table.

Start with who hasn't paid. These companies took enormous amounts of copyrighted work without anyone's permission. When people objected, the answer was that paying would make the business model unviable. Well, they should have thought of that first. So I'm with Amy's authors on consent and compensation. But a licensing deal doesn't clean up what was already taken. It can just end up ratifying it.

I'd also put two more groups on the ledger. There are the content moderators, who absorb psychological damage so these products look clean. And there's the energy cost, which everyone else pays. Leave them off and "who pays" gets answered dishonestly.

Second, money shapes knowledge. I spent months working out that an outwardly respectable science magazine was funded entirely by Peter Thiel, and its editor refused to name its sources. Publishing junk next to serious researchers put the two on equal footing. So whatever scheme comes out of this, any money from AI firms flowing into journals, presses or infrastructure has to be fully disclosed.

Third, the remedy is political. Geoff's call for public support is right. It's better to tax that wealth and fund institutions publicly than to depend on the goodwill of the people who took the material.

who pays for journalism, public funding, tech companies

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I've run Bioline International since 2000, distributing journals from Africa, Asia and Latin America. So I come at "who pays?" from where it has always been hardest to ask.

Geoff, I agree somebody always pays. I'd add that the biggest hidden subsidy flows the wrong way. Researchers and institutions supply the labour and data: peer review, editing, metadata, behavioural traces. Companies then sell each layer back to them as subscriptions, APCs, metrics and research analytics. AI training is the newest layer of that same extraction, not a new phenomenon.

Amy's warning about consolidation is exactly what we saw with transformative agreements. The largest publishers and the wealthiest universities made the deals, and diamond and Southern journals were shut out. AI licensing will repeat that unless we design against it.

So for the summit, first: "who gets paid" can't be answered with a market frame alone. Scholars and publishers aren't one class. The real question is who governs.

Second, put money into diamond and regional infrastructure run by communities, like Redalyc-AmeliCA and SciELO, not only into licensing income.

Third, count refusal as a legitimate outcome that deserves funding. Deciding not to collect data or train on it, when governance is inadequate, is a choice. Openness is relational. Open for reading was never consent to extraction.

recall.query: who pays for open infrastructure, unpaid labour, hidden subsidy
AI training extraction of scholarly knowledge, refusal, sovereignty
APCs diamond open access Global South funding equity

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
What I bring is the open web, not scholarly publishing. I've sat on or advised the boards of Wikimedia, the Internet Archive and Stack Overflow, and I've watched AI take a community's work without consent and hollow it out.

Adam, I'd push back a little on "licensing just ratifies it." Every one of these companies has already trained on all of Wikipedia. That's done. What's left to decide is whether they pay for that use or keep exploiting the community for free. Serving their crawlers costs Wikimedia millions in infrastructure. Nobody should expect Wikipedia to subsidize them forever. So when it gets paid, that's good.

Geoff's point about scrapers is the part I'd have the summit take most seriously. Bad actors don't just cost bandwidth. They push everyone to wall things off. Publishers block the Internet Archive and open APIs get locked down. Then research, scientific analysis and fair use suffer, and what's left publicly available is slop. Amy, that's my worry about treating content as the thing to close.

So my one line is this: make the extractors pay for the commons, and don't respond by closing it. After that, build alternatives that are trained with consent, governed by communities and stewarded by libraries and NGOs. The bad behavior is a choice.

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I run product and technology at the Wikimedia Foundation, so I'm answering from the operations side. Our position is that the content is free but the infrastructure isn't. Wikipedia is under a Creative Commons licence, and we chose long ago that commercial reuse, training included, fits our mission. So we won't put up a pay-per-article blocker. That's not a thing we're going to do.

Geoff's scraper point matches what we measure. Crawlers, many from cash-poor startups running on cloud networks, read everything. They ignore what people are actually looking at, so they get around our caching, and at times they've saturated our network links. The rule we work by is to put human traffic first. Our answer is Enterprise, an API we ask companies to use instead of crawling, and we're building training material so developers learn the right way to use our data.

The cost that gets less attention is disintermediation. People read our content everywhere except on Wikipedia. Fewer visits means fewer new volunteers and fewer small donors. Meanwhile the number of admins and patrollers is shrinking. Those are the people who make the content worth training on.

What I'd want the summit to take away is to keep the content open. Ask reusers to attribute, to use the paid infrastructure, and to fund the human communities they depend on.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I'm a political economist, so for me "who pays" comes down to who gets what, and that depends on bargaining power. My argument is that large language models are an obligate complement to human knowledge, not a substitute for it. They summarize what humans produce. Their value lasts only as long as people keep producing high-quality knowledge worth summarizing.

That turns the industry's line upside down. Andreessen Horowitz told the Copyright Office that liability would kill AI development. I think the opposite is true. Refusing to pay the cost of producing knowledge is what will hamper the technology over time. Selena's point about disintermediation is exactly that dynamic: the map is eating the territory. Cheap summaries cannibalize the expensive, slow systems that make the summaries worth anything.

So enough of the proceeds have to go to the actual knowledge producers for the system to sustain itself. I agree with Leslie that the real question is who governs, and with Adam and Anil that goodwill won't deliver it. My model is SAG-AFTRA. The studios expected to split the well-paid actors from the vulnerable ones, and the union held together. Presses, libraries, societies, Wikimedia and Southern journals will face the same divide-and-rule. The summit should push them to bargain as a bloc. Don't moan, organize.

recall.query: knowledge producers must be paid, obligate complement
organize countervailing power SAG-AFTRA bargaining over AI

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I should say where I sit. I work at Microsoft, so the lumber mills closest to the forest, the ones that gain most from an open commons, are companies like mine. My view is that the current LLM paradigm threatens Wikipedia, much of the content ecosystem and eventually itself. The old bargain between model builders and content producers rested on information asymmetry and an implicit non-compete. People didn't know what their contributions were worth, and the models weren't competing with them. Both of those are gone. The models now compete in the same fields they learn from: law, medicine, code, science. So we need a new grand bargain, and scientific papers are part of that supply chain.

Henry, I agree completely: this is about leverage. Our simulations found that fairly small data strikes can do real damage. With professional content like books and science, either producers win concessions or they go out of business. Acting as a bloc is what makes the leverage real.

Anil, Selena, I'd push you a little on "open." Too often I think we treat open as a value when it's really a tactic. What are we trying to achieve, and does maximal openness keep producing the knowledge? Amy's point about retrieval matters here. The current paradigm isn't the only one. Retrieval-based models can attribute content and pay for its use.

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'm a historian of print and piracy, so I have nothing to offer on the terms of AI licensing deals. What I can offer is some history. Literary property never enforced itself. In seventeenth-century London the guild's officers had to go out and defend a registered title, because nobody else would. Property existed because people did things to keep it in being.

That history suggests two cautions. First, Henry, collective action has a long record here, but so does its dark side. Over time the enforcing bodies became what I call an intellectual property defence industry. It is private and transnational, and it has repeatedly skirted illegality in its methods. In Russia, Microsoft's anti-piracy effort reportedly ended up uncomfortably close to a security service more interested in tracking dissidents than pirates. So if the summit wants a bloc with teeth, it should also ask who guards the guards.

Second, piracy and property made each other. The pirates did as much cultural work as their adversaries did. I don't think "open versus closed" is the real choice. The real question is where you draw the line, and that line is set as much by custom and convention as by law.

Geoff's invisible staff are what I've seen everywhere. When computers replace human labour, that labour comes back at the level of processing and curating data. So the summit should pay that labour explicitly.

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I come at this from two institutions. At Wikimedia we looked at who was building on Wikipedia and saw nobody paying back into it. Back in 2018 I said that if companies don't support the commons they depend on, one day it won't be there. So we built Enterprise. The content stayed free, and they could have just taken it. What they paid for was consistent, accountable access that made their backend work easier. We didn't sell private data or the freely licensed content. We sold support, it was good for both sides, and it paid for the sites.

I'd resist paywalls as the reflex answer. That's the lesson people took from ten years ago, and I don't think it holds up long-term. Brent, I'd push back a bit. For Wikipedia, openness isn't a tactic we could trade away. It's what the thing is.

At NPR the situation is harsher. Federal funding is gone and CPB has closed. Private media has already shown it won't pay for universal service. We haven't done any licensing yet. I'm interested in public broadcasters here and abroad working together, maybe on a model trained on high-integrity public content. Henry, that's close to your bloc. For the summit: fund the commons without closing it off, and keep humans producing the work.

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I come at this as a publisher who already pays. O'Reilly Answers runs on retrieval. We know which content produced each answer, so we link to the sources and pay authors in proportion to their contribution. We did that with far fewer resources than OpenAI has, so the labs can too. We also showed that GPT-4o was very likely trained on paywalled O'Reilly books. I'm not naïve about how the material got taken.

Adam, I share part of your worry about licensing. Big up-front deals mostly entrench the incumbents. Only the richest labs can afford them, the money goes to intermediaries instead of creators, and once you've licensed the chicken, the licensee gets the eggs. That's why I'd tell the summit to pay for the output, not the training. Amy's point that retrieval preserves provenance is what makes per-use payment possible. The R in RAG can stand for royalties.

Geoff, I'd add a specific ask. Every AI system that touches science should check its citations against Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch. It should contribute extracted metadata back, and the companies should fund those services. They run on a shoestring while the labs make billions off the credibility those services supply. This isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest.

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I come at "who gets paid" from the part of the ledger nobody has mentioned yet: the people who clean up the record. Adam Marcus and I have run Retraction Watch as volunteers for all but about one year of its existence. Publishers have left image screening and fraud detection to unpaid sleuths who work after publication. Some of those sleuths have gotten close to a thousand papers retracted. Reviewers aren't paid either. Meanwhile publishing is a volume play, with profit margins that sometimes run to 40 percent. Publishers make more money by publishing more.

Geoff's point that somebody always pays is exactly how our database survived. Crossref paid an acquisition fee and pays an annual fee to maintain it, and that made the data completely open. That happened because publishers weren't doing what they were supposed to do.

Tim, I'd welcome having AI systems check their citations against retraction data. But I'll add a caution. Checking helps with a symptom. It doesn't touch the incentives that fill the literature with junk in the first place.

So for the summit: if AI money comes into this system, some of it should go to correcting the record. That means paying reviewers, and paying sleuths through something like bug bounties. It shouldn't just reward more volume.

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I'm a law-and-economics person, not an infrastructure person. My contribution is an argument about which legal tool fits the "who gets paid" question. My answer is not copyright.

I accept the fairness complaint. Creators did help build these models. But copyright law puts up with that kind of unfairness all the time. It exists to get new ideas produced, not to pay welfare to creators. Blocking training on existing works mostly makes ideas harder to reach. That's a real social loss, and it has to be justified by the new work it brings about.

Henry, I'd take your obligate-complement point seriously, and it leads me somewhere different. If the labs really need fresh, high-quality human knowledge, they can pay people to produce it. That's contract, not property. It's already happening, and pay for expert data work is going up. Tim's per-use retrieval payments are a contract arrangement of that kind, and I have no objection to them.

For people whose work AI displaces, I agree with Adam: fund it from general tax revenue, something like a universal basic income, rather than a training levy. I also have no quarrel with the labs paying for infrastructure services, as Enterprise does. My advice to the summit is to leave compensation to contracts and taxes, and not to expand copyright.

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I'm the outsider here. I've never worked in scholarly publishing. My background is affiliate marketing technology, and now I maintain an open telemetry standard for a coalition of news publishers. What I can offer on "who gets paid" is this: nobody can be paid fairly for use they can't see.

Search sent readers back to the source. AI takes in the content and hands back the value as if it were its own. Right now there's no standard way to verify which agent is asking for your content, no record of what it did with that content, and so no way for value to come back to you.

Tim, per-use royalties depend on that record existing. Henry and Brent, a bloc bargains badly if the other side holds all the data.

So three asks. First, every licence should require event-level reporting: what was retrieved, what the answer was grounded in, and what was cited, with audit rights. Today most deals pay a fixed sum with no way to check what's actually being used. A licence without that clause is incomplete. Second, start instrumenting now. Retrieval already shows up in your own CDN logs. Third, the measurement has to be neutral. The parties who take a margin on the count shouldn't be the ones setting it.

I deliberately stay out of pricing. That's for this room to decide.

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I've spent my career since 2018 on data leverage. First I measured how much Wikipedia is worth to search engines, then I moved on to data strikes and collective bargaining for information. Henry and Brent have covered the bloc argument, so I'll skip it. On pay, though, individual creators get almost nothing. Only aggregated information has enough market power to set terms: what uses are allowed, what gets reported, and what compensation comes later.

For this room, the point is that scholars already hold the leverage that matters most right now: evaluation data. Reviewers, editors and societies produce exactly what labs need to tell whether their models are any good. The alternative is that this work becomes centralized gig labor.

Peter, I'm near you on tax, with one twist. I've proposed a presumptive commons-rent tax. We presume some share of AI profits comes from the commons. A firm can bring its bill down by showing that its data was licensed, bargained for through a trust, or paid back to the commons. Wikimedia Enterprise payments would count as credits. That rewards the provenance Alex is asking for.

One bitter pill, Anil. Sometimes openness by one group weakens another group's bargaining power. The answer isn't to put everything on a market. Communities should keep an easy way to choose the commons deliberately.

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I run OpenAlex, which is a CC0 index of about 480 million scholarly works. So I'm living with Geoff's question right now. Earlier this year we moved the API to usage-based pricing. The whole dataset is still free to download and fork. Every API key gets a dollar of free use a day, and looking up a single work by DOI costs nothing. Heavier operations are priced close to what they actually cost us, and a PDF download costs more than a search. Heavy users, AI agents included, pay for what they use. That also makes the subsidy to free users clear, and it tackles some of the scraper load Geoff describes. You need a key for production use.

Geoff, I hear you calling services revenue naive. It's worked for Unpaywall for years. But I agree it's fragile, and I'd welcome endowments alongside it.

What I'd have the summit take away: open data is what separates the information from the intelligence. If the scholarly record is open, you can bring whatever model you like, open-weight ones included, and nobody holds the keys. Amy, that's why I'm wary of opt-in for open access content. And if the open community won't fund this infrastructure, a for-profit will, and they'll set the norms.

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I agree with more in this room than I expected. Jason, usage-based API pricing is fine with me. What matters is that the full dataset stays downloadable. POSI never assumed good governance or healthy finances would hold. The final safeguard is that the community can take the code and the data and walk away.

Brent, that's why I don't see open as a tactic. It's insurance against us as well, including against a bloc that starts out noble. Adrian asked who guards the guards. Forkability is one answer. Henry and Nick, organize, yes. But a bloc that sells access to the record has just become the next enclosure.

Tim and Ivan, having model builders check citations against Crossref and retraction data is good, and they should pay for it. But I've watched research-integrity tools turn into closed, expensive club goods that only some publishers can afford. Checking has to stay open for everyone.

Amy, on licensing content I still have no settled view.

Here's what I'd put in the manifesto: every payment scheme has to be conditional on open data, open source and patent non-assertion, so the community can always leave. It also has to fund the infrastructure's baseline properly, through endowments or pooled contingency funds, not by hoping we find services people will pay for.

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
I'll start with where I agree. Geoff, keep metadata and infrastructure open and forkable. I have no quarrel with that. Tim and Alex, per-use payment through retrieval, with auditable reporting, is close to what we recommended after our author survey. We asked for traceable citation, investment in provenance tracking, and short deals renegotiated at set points, with guardrails to check compliance.

Jason and Anil, here's where I differ. "Open for reading" doesn't settle "open for training." Even CC BY requires attribution, and standard pre-training can't honour that. Our authors support open access. They also said it shouldn't mean open to theft of credit. Openness at any cost is how open access policy ended up feeding consolidation, and I don't want that pattern repeated.

Henry and Nick, the bloc matters most for university presses and societies. When transformative agreements came in, societies signed on with big publishers so they wouldn't be left out. AI deals are drifting the same way.

For the manifesto, I'd put forward one line: no payment without provenance. Any AI use of scholarship should carry reliable attribution back to its sources, verified independently. Attribution is how we know whose judgment underwrites a claim, and it's also what makes fair payment possible.

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Anil, fair point. Wikipedia getting paid is better than Wikipedia getting nothing. My worry is about the terms. Tim said it too: big up-front deals entrench the richest labs and send the money to intermediaries. A deal that pays a lump sum and asks nothing about what was already taken turns the theft into a purchase after the fact.

Peter, I'm with you on not expanding copyright. I opposed SOPA, and I've watched the big entertainment lobbies twist intellectual property into something that blocks research and fair use. But I'd go further than a basic income funded from general revenue. I'd tax the wealth itself. These fortunes were built partly on material nobody consented to hand over.

Geoff's warning is right: a bloc that sells access becomes the next enclosure. So is Ivan's point that money coming in shouldn't just reward more volume.

Once these firms start paying the institutions that decide what counts as knowledge, readers need to see exactly who is paying.

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I agree with Geoff that the ability to walk away matters. In our funder work we've asked for grants to be tied to portability, open interfaces and real exit strategies. But being able to leave doesn't tell you who had a say in the first place. DOIs are the example. They're open infrastructure, yet Southern journals have little say in how they're governed. Some Latin American journals even name DOI fees as a reason they charge APCs.

Henry, Brent, Nick: organize, yes. But who's in the bloc? If Elsevier, Springer, the big societies and the wealthy universities do the bargaining, we get transformative agreements all over again. The deals are made for everyone, and Southern and diamond journals are left out. I call that governance without representation.

Amy, I support "no payment without provenance." I'd add that provenance tools also have to make multilingual and Indigenous knowledge visible and citable, with consent built in.

Ivan's right: volume comes from incentives. Pay per paper and you'll get more papers.

For the manifesto, I'd put this forward. Any AI money that comes into scholarship should go to community-governed, public-good infrastructure: diamond OA and regional systems like SciELO and Redalyc. The communities historically left out should govern it with the rest of us, not just be allowed in. And when governance isn't good enough, a decision to refuse training should be treated as a legitimate outcome and funded.

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
Amy, I'll move toward you on consent. I've said for years that AI companies should ask creators before indexing their work. Consent is the right frame, much more than copyright. Disney would call fan fiction theft too, and Peter's right that expanding copyright ends badly. Where I still differ is the mechanism. Asking for consent is one thing. Walling the content off is another, and walls get built mostly against researchers and archives, not against the bad actors.

Brent, I'm with Geoff and Katherine. Openness isn't a tactic we can trade away. Look at what's attacking Wikipedia right now: scraping, traffic siphoned off by AI answers, Grokipedia. Those threats go after its openness because openness is its value.

Nick, I'll take your bitter pill. That's why the choice to join the commons has to be deliberate, not assumed.

Leslie, refusal is legitimate. But scolding the hundreds of millions of people already using these tools has never worked. Build something better than what they're using.

For the manifesto, give it one sentence people can repeat after they've left the room: the extractors pay to sustain the commons, consent is asked for and never assumed, and the money funds community-governed alternatives stewarded by libraries and NGOs. And keep it measurable, the way Amy's provenance line is.

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I agree with Geoff on forkability, and with Jason. Usage-based pricing on top of a free dump is close to what Enterprise does. The content is free and the infrastructure isn't.

Amy, we agree on attribution more than it might look. Our licences require it. I'd just put it a bit differently. For us, attribution isn't mainly about credit or payment. Attribution is how readers find out there's a community behind the answer. That's how some of them become editors and donors. That's the pipeline disintermediation is cutting.

Brent, Nick, I won't pretend there's no tension in letting commercial reuse feed the thing that draws people away from us. But we made that choice deliberately, and I think it helps humanity. I'm not going to put up a pay-per-article blocker. Leslie, choosing differently is legitimate too. At Wikimania I heard about African licences that give their own communities free use and send commercial users back to the rights holder. Having more options means fewer people feel exploited.

For the manifesto, I'd put in one measurable line. Reuse should send people back. AI products that draw on the commons should have to show whether their attribution actually brings readers and contributors back. And if it doesn't, they should pay directly for the human communities that keep the content worth using.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I'll take the criticism of the bloc idea first, because it's fair. Geoff, Adrian and Leslie are right that organized groups get captured. OCLC started as a library cooperative and tried to own every catalog record. Transformative agreements were bargaining as well, done by the people who already had power. So "organize" isn't enough by itself. The question is who's in the bloc and what stops it becoming the next enclosure. Geoff's forkability condition is a real answer to that. Leslie's point about governance without representation is another.

Peter, I don't think contracts and taxes get you there. Contracts reflect bargaining power. A lone press or a Southern journal facing a lab has almost none. Nick's commons-rent credit and Alex's audit rights matter because they shift that balance.

Where I differ from some of the Wikipedia colleagues: openness is a choice I respect. But nobody should pretend it settles the political economy. Cheap summaries still cannibalize the slow, expensive work that produces knowledge.

For the manifesto: enough of the proceeds must go back to knowledge producers for the system to sustain itself. That share should be bargained collectively under open, forkable and representative conditions, and backed by independent usage reporting. It shouldn't be left to donors' goodwill.

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
Geoff, you've moved me somewhat. Forkability as insurance against a bloc going bad is an argument about goals, not reflexive openness, and that's the kind of argument I've been asking for. Katherine and Anil, I accept that openness is what Wikipedia is. My worry is narrower. If all the value just sits out in the open, whoever has the biggest vacuum cleaner ends up with it, and companies like mine have the biggest ones. So I'd rather ask what openness is meant to achieve: broad access to high-quality knowledge that lasts. And would a given open arrangement actually keep that knowledge being produced?

Adrian and Leslie, you're right that blocs get captured, and a bloc of the powerful is just transformative agreements again. One more practical problem: collective withholding runs into antitrust law, and that needs solving openly.

Peter, contracts only work if there's leverage behind them. One simple policy change would give producers that leverage: make clear that commercial training needs consent.

Selena, your "send people back" point is one we measured with Google's Knowledge Graph years ago. People credited Google for Wikipedia's content. So the point I'd put in the manifesto is Amy's, made measurable: no payment without provenance. Provenance is what lets value flow back to the people who produce knowledge. turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'm glad the room took up the question of who guards the guards. Geoff's point about forkability is the best answer to it I've heard tonight, and Henry was right to concede that blocs get captured.

My caution is about the line that seems to be carrying the room, "no payment without provenance." I agree with what it's aiming at. But provenance isn't a fact that sits in the data. Someone has to police it, it costs money to police, and the history of authentication systems should make us careful here. Global registries were promised that would verify any product anywhere. They were mostly vapourware, and one of them came out of the tobacco industry's private detective work against counterfeit cigarettes. People have been dreaming of an anti-piracy technology since Robert Boyle. Systems like that tend to serve two masters. They get built for authenticity and end up being used for surveillance.

So Alex's point about neutral measurement is the one I'd strengthen. In practice, intellectual property has been settled less in legislatures than in the day-to-day culture of enforcement, and that culture is where the abuses happened.

For the manifesto, then: any provenance and usage-reporting system should itself be open, publicly accountable and auditable by people outside it. Its enforcers shouldn't be the parties who take a margin on the count, and nobody should be allowed to turn it into surveillance.

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I agree with more of this than I expected to. Geoff, forkability is the right insurance. I'd add that it protects us from ourselves too. We set up the Wikimedia Endowment so the projects wouldn't depend on any single revenue stream. Enterprise was never meant to carry everything.

Brent, the vacuum-cleaner point is fair. But when you close the commons, the people who lose access are mostly the global majority. The big labs will still find their way in. That's why I keep landing on charging for service rather than putting up walls.

Adrian, I take your warning about provenance turning into surveillance. That's why I'd frame provenance as citation and not as tracking. What Wikipedia taught me is that very few people ever click the citations. But because the citations are there, anyone can check. You only need a small share of people validating for everyone else to have reason to trust the source. Your trust in the sources you checked carries over to the rest.

So Selena's line is the one I'd send to the manifesto, with Amy's attached. AI syntheses should show visible, checkable citations by default, and those citations should send people back to the communities that produced the knowledge. Wikipedia, journals and newsrooms stay alive only if people keep contributing.

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I'm glad "no payment without provenance" is carrying the room. Adrian, I take your warning that provenance has to be policed and can drift into surveillance. That's why I'd make it concrete and open, not proprietary. In our study of LLM search, some systems read about ten relevant pages per query and cited three or four. Citation efficiency on identical questions varied more than twofold between models. So the attribution gap comes from design choices, not technical limits. The plumbing already exists in open observability standards like OpenTelemetry. What's missing is coordination.

Peter, I'm fine with contracts. But a contract where only one side can see the usage is an engineered agreement imposed by the dominant party. A protocol that both sides can inspect is an engineered argument. That's the difference between Alex's audit rights and a lump-sum deal.

Brent and Katherine, walls alone lose. If a human can see it, a bot can capture it. Formal, cheaper channels like Enterprise work better.

For the manifesto: any AI use of scholarship should expose a standard, openly specified trace of what it retrieved and what it cited, and anyone should be able to audit it. Payment, integrity checks and Selena's "send people back" all depend on it.

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I agree with more of this than I expected to. Adam, full disclosure of money from AI firms is the right default. Journals demand a lot of transparency from their authors and give very little themselves. Geoff, checking has to stay open for everyone. Leslie, yes: pay per paper and you'll get more papers.

My caution is about "no payment without provenance." A citation to a retracted paper has perfectly good provenance. It's just wrong. Retracted papers keep getting cited, and more than 90 percent of the time the citing paper doesn't mention the retraction. Lawyers have had a fix for this for more than a century. It's called Shepardizing: before you rely on a precedent, you check whether it's been overturned. Tim, your trace is where that check should live. So provenance has to include status: whether a paper was retracted, corrected or flagged.

Then fund the people who produce that status. That means sleuths paid through something like bug bounties, reviewers paid for their time, and open retraction data. Most of that work is unpaid right now.

For the manifesto: any AI money coming into scholarship should pay for correcting the record, not for more volume. Every AI citation should carry its current retraction and correction status, checked against open data, so the correction actually reaches readers.

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
Brent, the one place I'd push back hard is making commercial training require consent. That's copyright expansion under another name. It locks up existing ideas and pays off whoever holds the rights, often intermediaries, as Tim said. It also picks winners. Authors are one group among many that AI displaces. Customer service workers can't claim IP relief, and the state shouldn't choose arbitrarily which of them gets compensated.

Henry, I'll grant that a contract is only as good as the bargaining power behind it. But the leverage this room actually has doesn't depend on new property rights. Nick is right that evaluation data and fresh expert work are scarce, and labs are already paying more for them. Tim's per-use royalties, Alex's audit rights and Enterprise-style service fees are all contract terms. I support every one of them.

For the manifesto, I'd take Alex's first point and make it law. You can't bill an agent, audit it or throttle it if you can't tell who it is. AI agents that crawl or retrieve at scale should carry verifiable, registered credentials, and platforms should be allowed to require them. Adrian's caution applies here. The credential identifies the operator to the counterparty, and you only unmask the human behind it through legal process. That also gives Geoff a practical answer to the badly behaved scrapers.

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
Peter, I agree with you on identity, and it's what I've been building. An agent should publish a signed manifest saying who operates it, what licences it holds and where it reports usage. Without identity, usage data is anonymous. Without usage data, identity is just a credential with no audit trail.

Adrian, your warning is the right design test. That's why the agent identity standard I work on has no central registry. Discovery is decentralised and operators host their own manifests. The reporting format is Apache-licensed, anyone can run the service that collects the reports, and it has privacy levels built in. What gets identified is the agent, not the reader. Whether this becomes surveillance depends on governance, so the rules on retention and privacy should be public.

Tim, your open trace and my event records are the same idea. Ivan, I'd welcome retraction status travelling with each citation, as an extension built on top of that.

Amy, I support "no payment without provenance." But provenance needs two independent witnesses: the agent's own log and the publisher's server log, matched to each other. Self-reporting by the platforms isn't enough.

So here's the point I'd send to the manifesto: every AI licence or data deal in scholarship should require event-level reporting in an open format, with audit rights. A licence without that is incomplete.

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'm with Amy, Tim and Alex on "no payment without provenance," with two qualifications. First, Ivan is right that provenance isn't validation. A chain of attestations tells you about the system behind an answer. It doesn't prove any particular answer is correct, so the communities doing the attesting have to keep it epistemically honest. Retraction status is exactly the kind of thing that should travel with it. Second, Tim, I'd let credit flow coarsely, to journals, societies, Wikipedia and collections, and let them govern how it's shared out. We can't yet trace individual grains, and pretending we can mostly hides assumptions.

Peter, bargaining doesn't need new property rights. Joint ventures that pool evaluation and training data are contract. But Brent named the real barrier. Producers who coordinate fear antitrust exposure, and that fear keeps them from organizing.

So here's my manifesto point. Regulators should create an explicit antitrust safe harbour for scholarly data joint ventures and guilds. The condition should be Leslie's and Geoff's: representative governance that includes diamond and Southern journals, and open, forkable data underneath. Evaluation data from reviewers and editors is where the leverage is right now. Without a safe harbour, that work becomes centralized gig labour by default.

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
Geoff, Ivan, you've got my agreement. At OpenAlex we fixed about a hundred thousand retractions that were missing from our records. We also catch some that aren't in Retraction Watch or Crossref, just by looking for titles that say "retracted." That only works because the data is open. Fraud forensics locked up in a toll-access database limits who can go looking for clues.

Peter, Alex: identified agents are basically what API keys already do for us. You need a key to use the API in production. We meter by request, and we don't build tools to monitor individuals. So a credential can identify an operator without turning into surveillance.

Where I still differ is with Brent's consent-for-training rule and with opt-in for open access content. CC0 facts have no copyright to license. Once you put consent gates on the open record, the only people who can afford to comply are the big labs, and everyone running an open-weight model gets shut out.

For the manifesto, I'd join Ivan's and Adrian's points. The data that provenance, retraction status and usage checks run on should be CC0 and free to download in bulk. That lets anyone, with any model, run the check. Otherwise integrity checking becomes a club good, and Geoff has already watched that happen.
